questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Which nuclear features characterise papillary thyroid carcinoma on histology?
options: Optically clear ground-glass nuclei with grooves and intranuclear pseudoinclusions, with psammoma bodies
Small round nuclei with follicles and capsular invasion
questions.concept: The diagnosis rests on these nuclear features rather than on papillae alone, and the tumour spreads by lymphatics yet carries an excellent prognosis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Endocrine System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Which combination defines multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A, and which gene is responsible?
options: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia, caused by a germline RET mutation
Parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours from a MEN1 mutation
Medullary thyroid carcinoma with mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus
Phaeochromocytoma with haemangioblastoma from a VHL mutation
questions.concept: Identifying a RET mutation permits prophylactic thyroidectomy in childhood, and phaeochromocytoma must always be excluded before any surgery to avoid an intraoperative hypertensive crisis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Endocrine System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Which adrenal lesion causes hypertension with hypokalaemia and a suppressed renin, and what is its typical appearance?
options: An aldosterone-producing cortical adenoma, small and golden-yellow on section
questions.concept: Bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia is now recognised as commoner than the classic Conn adenoma, and the distinction matters because hyperplasia is treated medically rather than surgically.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Endocrine System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Which histological feature identifies a phaeochromocytoma, and what determines its malignancy?
options: Nests of chromaffin cells in a zellballen pattern, with malignancy defined only by metastasis rather than by histology
Amyloid stroma, with malignancy defined by mitoses
Papillae, with malignancy defined by capsular invasion
Clear cells, with malignancy defined by nuclear grade
questions.concept: Because no histological feature reliably predicts behaviour, all such tumours are followed long term, and about a quarter are associated with a germline mutation.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Endocrine System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Which pituitary pathology causes hypopituitarism with an enlarged sella and a raised prolactin that is only modestly elevated?
options: A non-functioning macroadenoma compressing the stalk, producing the stalk section effect
questions.concept: A prolactin of a few thousand indicates a true prolactinoma whereas a level of 50 to 100 with a large mass indicates compression, and the distinction determines whether a dopamine agonist or surgery is appropriate.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Endocrine System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Which thyroid pathology is associated with a raised serum calcitonin and amyloid deposition in the stroma?
options: Medullary carcinoma, arising from neural crest-derived parafollicular C cells
questions.concept: The amyloid is derived from procalcitonin, the tumour does not take up radioiodine because it is not of follicular origin, and carcinoembryonic antigen with calcitonin is used for follow-up.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Endocrine System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: GIT: PUD, IBD, colorectal carcinoma, malabsorption
questions.stem: Which sequence describes the commonest molecular pathway to sporadic colorectal carcinoma?
options: The chromosomal instability pathway with APC loss, then KRAS activation and TP53 loss
The microsatellite instability pathway with mismatch repair loss
The serrated pathway with BRAF mutation
questions.concept: Familial adenomatous polyposis is the germline model of this pathway, whereas Lynch syndrome follows the mismatch repair route and tends to produce right-sided, poorly differentiated, mucinous tumours.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Gastrointestinal Tract

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: GIT: PUD, IBD, colorectal carcinoma, malabsorption
questions.stem: Which pathological features distinguish Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis?
options: Transmural inflammation with skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, fissures and fistulae
Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum with crypt abscesses
questions.concept: Because Crohn disease affects the full thickness it produces strictures and fistulae, whereas ulcerative colitis remains mucosal so it produces bleeding, pseudopolyps and a higher risk of dysplasia in long-standing disease.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Gastrointestinal Tract

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: GIT: PUD, IBD, colorectal carcinoma, malabsorption
questions.stem: Which histological finding in a duodenal biopsy indicates coeliac disease?
options: Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
questions.concept: Periodic acid-Schiff-positive macrophages indicate Whipple disease, and the changes of coeliac disease are graded by the Marsh classification and reverse on a gluten-free diet.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Gastrointestinal Tract

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: GIT: PUD, IBD, colorectal carcinoma, malabsorption
questions.stem: Which gastric pathology carries the greatest risk of gastric adenocarcinoma?
options: Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia, usually from Helicobacter pylori
questions.concept: Duodenal ulcer disease with high acid output is actually associated with a reduced gastric cancer risk, whereas the atrophic corpus-predominant pattern with hypochlorhydria is the high-risk phenotype.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Gastrointestinal Tract

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: GIT: PUD, IBD, colorectal carcinoma, malabsorption
questions.stem: Which polyp type carries essentially no malignant potential yet may be numerous in a syndrome associated with cancer elsewhere?
options: Hamartomatous polyps of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, where the cancer risk arises from other organs and from associated adenomas
questions.concept: Understanding which polyps are precursors and which are markers determines surveillance strategy, and juvenile polyposis and Cowden syndrome pose comparable interpretive problems.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Gastrointestinal Tract

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: GIT: PUD, IBD, colorectal carcinoma, malabsorption
questions.stem: Why does a right-sided colonic carcinoma present differently from a left-sided one?
options: The wider caecal lumen allows exophytic growth with occult bleeding and anaemia, whereas the narrower left colon produces annular obstruction and altered bowel habit
questions.concept: This anatomical difference, together with distinct molecular pathways, explains why an unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult demands colonic investigation.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Gastrointestinal Tract

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains the variable severity of a mitochondrial disorder within one family?
options: Heteroplasmy, with the proportion of mutant mitochondrial genomes varying between cells and tissues
questions.concept: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited so affected mothers transmit to all children, but the threshold effect of mutant load explains why phenotype varies so widely.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Genetic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which phenomenon explains why Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes result from the same chromosomal deletion?
options: Genomic imprinting, with the phenotype depending on whether the deleted 15q11-13 region is of paternal or maternal origin
questions.concept: Paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy gives Prader-Willi, and maternal deletion or paternal disomy gives Angelman, which is why methylation testing rather than karyotype alone is used.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Genetic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which molecular mechanism accounts for the increasing severity of myotonic dystrophy in successive generations?
options: Anticipation from expansion of a CTG trinucleotide repeat during transmission
questions.concept: The same phenomenon occurs in Huntington disease and fragile X syndrome, and the repeat length correlates with age of onset and severity.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Genetic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which finding on a karyotype indicates a Robertsonian translocation as the cause of Down syndrome, and why does it matter?
options: Fusion of the long arms of chromosome 21 with another acrocentric chromosome, because a parent may be a balanced carrier with a high recurrence risk
questions.concept: About 4 percent of cases are translocation-related, and identifying a carrier parent transforms the recurrence risk from about 1 percent to as high as 15 percent, which changes counselling entirely.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Genetic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains why a female heterozygous for an X-linked disorder may be symptomatic?
options: Skewed X inactivation, so the mutant allele is active in a disproportionate share of cells
questions.concept: Lyonisation is random so most carriers are mosaic and asymptomatic, but skewing explains symptomatic carriers of Duchenne dystrophy, ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency and Fabry disease.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Genetic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does a mutation in a gene of a lysosomal enzyme produce a progressive storage disease rather than an acute presentation?
options: Undegraded substrate accumulates gradually within lysosomes until cellular function is compromised
The enzyme is required only in adulthood
questions.concept: The gradual accumulation explains the progressive course with a symptom-free interval and the correlation between residual enzyme activity and age of onset, and it is the rationale for enzyme replacement.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Genetic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which cell is the essential component of a granuloma, and what cytokine drives its formation?
options: The epithelioid macrophage, driven by interferon-gamma from Th1 lymphocytes
The plasma cell, driven by interleukin-6
questions.concept: Tumour necrosis factor maintains granuloma integrity, which is why its blockade reactivates latent tuberculosis and why screening precedes such therapy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Inflammation and Infectious Disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the granulomas of sarcoidosis from those of tuberculosis?
options: Non-caseating granulomas with no organisms in sarcoidosis, versus caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli in tuberculosis
Presence of giant cells in sarcoidosis only
questions.concept: Because sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion, special stains and culture must be negative, and asteroid and Schaumann bodies are supportive but not specific.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Inflammation and Infectious Disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which pathological sequence describes primary pulmonary tuberculosis?
options: A subpleural parenchymal focus with hilar node involvement forming the Ghon complex, which usually heals by fibrosis and calcification
questions.concept: Post-primary disease instead affects the apical and posterior segments where oxygen tension is highest, with cavitation from liquefaction of caseous material.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Inflammation and Infectious Disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which structure is characteristic of caseous necrosis on histology?
options: Amorphous granular eosinophilic debris with loss of cellular outline, enclosed by a granulomatous rim
Preserved cellular architecture with coagulated protein
questions.concept: The combination of coagulative and liquefactive change reflects the lipid-rich mycobacterial wall, and the cheesy gross appearance gives the name.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Inflammation and Infectious Disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does miliary tuberculosis produce nodules of uniform size throughout both lungs?
options: Simultaneous haematogenous seeding disseminates organisms to all regions at once, so all lesions are of the same age
questions.concept: The uniformity distinguishes it radiologically from bronchogenic spread, where lesions differ in age and size, and it reflects the moment of vascular breach.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Inflammation and Infectious Disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why can a granulomatous reaction occur without an infectious agent, and what is the mechanism?
options: Persistent poorly degradable material or a hypersensitivity reaction sustains macrophage activation, as with foreign bodies, berylliosis and Crohn disease
questions.concept: Foreign body granulomas differ in lacking the T cell-mediated component and in showing the material within giant cells under polarised light, which is why polarisation should always be attempted.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Inflammation and Infectious Disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Haemodynamics: oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock
questions.stem: Which components of Virchow's triad predispose to venous thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury, stasis or turbulent flow, and hypercoagulability
questions.concept: Venous thrombi arise mainly from stasis and hypercoagulability whereas arterial thrombi arise mainly from endothelial injury, which is why anticoagulants suit one and antiplatelets the other.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Hemodynamic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Haemodynamics: oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes an antemortem thrombus from a postmortem clot at autopsy?
options: Lines of Zahn with attachment to the vessel wall in an antemortem thrombus
questions.concept: The alternating pale platelet and fibrin layers with darker red cell layers indicate flowing blood at the time of formation, which is the pathological basis for distinguishing the two.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Hemodynamic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Haemodynamics: oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock
questions.stem: Which organ shows a haemorrhagic rather than a pale infarct, and why?
options: The lung, because of its dual blood supply and loose tissue permitting blood to seep into the infarcted area
The kidney, because it is highly vascular
The spleen, because of arterial supply
questions.concept: The intestine also produces haemorrhagic infarcts for the same reason, whereas solid organs with a single arterial supply and dense tissue produce pale wedge-shaped infarcts.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Hemodynamic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Haemodynamics: oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock
questions.stem: Which type of embolism should be suspected in a patient who becomes confused with petechiae and hypoxia 24 to 72 hours after a long bone fracture?
questions.concept: The latency, the triad of respiratory, neurological and cutaneous features and the association with marrow-containing fractures distinguish it from thromboembolism, which usually occurs later and without petechiae.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Hemodynamic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Haemodynamics: oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock
questions.stem: Which type of shock is characterised by a high cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance and warm peripheries?
options: Distributive shock, as in sepsis or anaphylaxis
questions.concept: The other three types share a low output with high resistance and cold peripheries, so recognising the warm phase of septic shock avoids the error of withholding fluid and vasopressor.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Hemodynamic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Haemodynamics: oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock
questions.stem: Why does chronic left heart failure produce haemosiderin-laden macrophages in the sputum?
options: Raised pulmonary capillary pressure causes microhaemorrhage, and alveolar macrophages phagocytose the red cells, becoming heart failure cells
questions.concept: The same process produces brown induration of the lung with fibrosis, and Prussian blue staining identifies the iron pigment within the macrophages.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Hemodynamic Disorders

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which type of hypersensitivity underlies the tuberculin skin reaction and contact dermatitis?
questions.concept: Because it depends on sensitised T cells recruiting macrophages rather than on antibody, it peaks at 48 to 72 hours and cannot be transferred with serum.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which mechanism of hypersensitivity explains Graves disease, and how does it differ from myasthenia gravis?
options: Type II with a stimulating antibody to the TSH receptor, whereas myasthenia has a blocking and destructive antibody to the acetylcholine receptor
questions.concept: Both are antibody-mediated diseases of receptors, and grouping them by mechanism rather than by organ explains why plasma exchange helps both and why neonatal transient disease can occur in each.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which pattern of amyloid deposition follows chronic inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or tuberculosis?
options: AA amyloid derived from serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein
AL amyloid derived from immunoglobulin light chains
questions.concept: Treating the underlying inflammation lowers serum amyloid A and can halt progression, which is why the distinction from AL amyloidosis of plasma cell dyscrasia matters therapeutically.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which organ involvement in amyloidosis most often determines prognosis, and how is it detected?
options: Cardiac involvement, detected by echocardiography showing a thickened non-dilated ventricle with a restrictive pattern and raised natriuretic peptides
questions.concept: Because cardiac amyloid carries the worst survival and is potentially treatable in transthyretin disease, its recognition drives both prognosis and access to specific therapy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which immunological mechanism explains why a single autoimmune disease can progressively involve more antigens over time?
options: Epitope spreading, in which tissue damage exposes new self antigens that recruit further immune responses
questions.concept: Combined with loss of regulatory T cell control and bystander activation, it explains why autoimmune disease tends to broaden and why early intervention may prevent that expansion.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does systemic lupus erythematosus produce such diverse organ involvement?
options: Circulating immune complexes deposit in many vascular beds, activating complement wherever they lodge
A single organ-specific antibody is responsible
It is a type IV reaction
It is caused by direct viral cytotoxicity
questions.concept: Complement consumption gives the low C3 and C4 of active disease, and immune complex deposition explains the glomerulonephritis, serositis, rash and arthritis together.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which primary immunodeficiency presents after 6 months of age with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infection and absent B cells?
options: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia from a BTK mutation
questions.concept: The delay reflects the protection of transplacental maternal IgG, and treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement with prompt antibiotic therapy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which immunodeficiency is characterised by recurrent infection with catalase-positive organisms and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine test?
options: Chronic granulomatous disease from NADPH oxidase deficiency
questions.concept: Phagocytes ingest but cannot kill, so granulomas form, and prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole, itraconazole and interferon-gamma reduces infection rates.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which type of transplant rejection is mediated by pre-formed antibody and occurs within minutes of anastomosis?
options: Hyperacute rejection, with thrombosis and immediate graft loss
questions.concept: Crossmatching to detect pre-formed donor-specific antibody is what prevents it, which is why ABO and HLA compatibility testing precede transplantation.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which histological finding indicates acute cellular rejection of a renal allograft?
options: A mononuclear interstitial infiltrate with tubulitis and sometimes endarteritis
questions.concept: Chronic rejection instead shows fibrosis with vascular intimal thickening and responds poorly to increased immunosuppression, so the Banff classification distinguishes them.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which HLA class presents antigen to CD8 T cells, and why is that relevant to viral infection?
options: Class I, expressed on all nucleated cells and presenting endogenously derived peptide to cytotoxic T cells
Class II, expressed on antigen presenting cells
questions.concept: Viruses replicating in any cell therefore present peptide on class I, which allows cytotoxic killing, and viral downregulation of class I is a common escape mechanism countered by natural killer cells.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does graft versus host disease occur after allogeneic bone marrow transplantation and not after solid organ transplantation?
options: Donor T cells in the graft recognise recipient tissue as foreign, and the recipient is immunosuppressed and cannot eliminate them
Recipient T cells attack the graft
questions.concept: Skin, gut and liver are the classic targets, and T cell depletion of the graft reduces the disease at the cost of a higher relapse rate because the graft versus leukaemia effect is also lost.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of the Immune System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which blast percentage in blood or marrow defines acute leukaemia in current classification?
options: Twenty percent or more blasts, or the presence of a defining genetic abnormality regardless of blast count
questions.concept: Certain recurrent abnormalities such as the t(15;17) or the core binding factor translocations are now diagnostic of acute myeloid leukaemia at any blast percentage, because their biology and treatment are defined by the genetics.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which stain distinguishes myeloid from lymphoid blasts on cytochemistry?
options: Myeloperoxidase positivity indicates myeloid lineage while periodic acid-Schiff block positivity suggests lymphoid
questions.concept: Flow cytometric immunophenotyping has largely replaced cytochemistry, but the principle of assigning lineage before treatment remains, because the therapy differs completely.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which chromosomal abnormality in acute myeloid leukaemia is associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation and responds to a differentiating agent?
options: The t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion of acute promyelocytic leukaemia, treated with all-trans retinoic acid
questions.concept: All-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide has converted the most lethal subtype into the most curable, and treatment begins on clinical suspicion because early haemorrhage kills.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which chronic leukaemia shows a markedly raised white cell count with the full spectrum of granulocytic maturation, a low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase and basophilia?
options: Chronic myeloid leukaemia with the BCR-ABL1 fusion
questions.concept: The distinction from a leukaemoid reaction rests on the fusion gene, the basophilia and the low alkaline phosphatase score, and tyrosine kinase inhibition has transformed survival.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which feature indicates transformation of chronic myeloid leukaemia to blast crisis?
options: Twenty percent or more blasts in blood or marrow with extramedullary disease and additional cytogenetic changes
questions.concept: Blast crisis may be myeloid or lymphoid, and its emergence despite tyrosine kinase inhibition usually reflects kinase domain mutations or clonal evolution.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which chronic lymphoid neoplasm shows cells with cytoplasmic projections, a dry marrow tap and splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy?
options: Hairy cell leukaemia, with a BRAF V600E mutation and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity
questions.concept: Marrow fibrosis explains the dry tap, and purine analogues such as cladribine produce prolonged remission, with BRAF inhibitors available for refractory disease.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which complication of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia presents with rapidly enlarging nodes, fever and a rising lactate dehydrogenase?
options: Richter transformation to diffuse large B cell lymphoma
questions.concept: Prognosis after transformation is poor, and it must be distinguished by biopsy from simple progression because the treatment approach differs entirely.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does a leukaemoid reaction need to be distinguished from chronic myeloid leukaemia, and how is this done?
options: Both raise the neutrophil count, but the leukaemoid reaction shows toxic granulation with a high alkaline phosphatase score and no BCR-ABL1 fusion
questions.concept: The reaction is a response to infection, inflammation or malignancy elsewhere and resolves with the cause, so molecular testing prevents both overtreatment and missed diagnosis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells
